profile.campus: Piscataway, Middlesex County, New Jersey (QTS Piscataway 1 campus)

source.basis: Operator facility page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

profile.reading:
QTS's own site describes this Piscataway, New Jersey facility, referred to as Piscataway 1, as sitting on a 38 acre campus at 101 Possumtown Road with more than 200 parking spaces, serving the greater New York City metro region. QTS states the campus carries more than 65 megawatts of total critical power capacity, a figure the company presents at the campus level rather than broken out for this specific building, so this registry records it as a campus wide figure rather than assigning it to a single structure. A separate two story, 50,000 square foot expansion building rated at 15 megawatts is also described on QTS's site as part of the same campus, confirming that more than one structure shares the published power total. QTS lists the campus as an Energy Star certified building and LEED Gold certified, running on utility sourced renewable power with a 2 megawatt rooftop solar field, an on site rainwater collection system, and dedicated electric vehicle charging spaces. QTS's page does not publish a year of construction, a technical space square footage for the main building alone, or any named tenant.

QTS was founded in 2003 in Overland Park, Kansas by Chad Williams, growing through acquisitions and ground up construction into a national wholesale and colocation platform, and went public as a real estate investment trust in 2013. That public period ended when Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust completed an acquisition of QTS valued at roughly 10 billion dollars on August 31, 2021, according to Blackstone's own press release, after which QTS stopped filing as an independent public company. QTS today markets itself as a hyperscale neutral wholesale and colocation landlord, leasing built data center capacity to enterprise, cloud, and hyperscale tenants rather than operating its own end user cloud service, a business model shared with peers such as Digital Realty and CyrusOne. Since the Blackstone acquisition, QTS has continued expanding across multiple United States metro areas, including large campus projects in the Phoenix and Dallas Fort Worth areas, rather than slowing its development pace.

Piscataway sits in Middlesex County, New Jersey, within the broader New York metro data center corridor that also includes the Equinix and other facilities tracked elsewhere in this registry, though QTS's Piscataway campus is positioned by the company as serving general enterprise and wholesale colocation demand rather than the low latency financial trading use case that characterizes the Secaucus area buildings closer to Manhattan.

reading.body:
The QTS Piscataway campus publishes 65 MW of IT capacity, making it the largest disclosed data center in New Jersey and accounting for roughly 69 percent of confirmed state capacity from operator spec pages.

New Jersey data center operators disclose power capacity selectively. Of 47 mapped facilities in the state, only two have published IT load figures. This opacity means the state's actual data center footprint is substantially unknown. What appears as Piscataway's dominance may reflect only QTS's willingness to publish, not the true distribution of power available to AI workloads across the region.

The 65 MW figure alone cannot reveal whether this campus suits dense AI training or general enterprise colocation. At 40 kW per rack, a typical density for GPU clusters, 65 MW supports roughly 1,625 racks. At 10 kW per rack, a common enterprise baseline, it supports 6,500. The operator publishes no cooling architecture, rack count, or power usage effectiveness metric, so the facility's actual suitability for compute-intensive workloads remains opaque. LEED Gold certification confirms environmental performance of the building envelope and systems, nothing about redundancy, uptime tier, or grid interconnection resilience.

Proximity to New York City and a 38-acre footprint with ongoing expansion signal regional infrastructure value. The gap between what the operator publishes and what AI infrastructure operators require for capacity planning demonstrates how incomplete public disclosure constrains visibility into the supply of dense compute real estate in high-density regions.
